readerTitle: Two texts, one Monday: why one team did the right job
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 회사, 철물점, 소프트웨어 팀) + 실제 연구 (Newton, 1990 두드리기 실험)
insight: 메시지가 명확한지는 내가 무엇을 말했는지가 아니라, 받는 사람이 되묻지 않고 바르게 행동할 수 있는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 내 머릿속에서 분명하면 상대에게도 분명하다. 자세히 길게 설명하거나 '신경 써 달라'고 강조하면 전달된다.

sources.text: Newton, E. L. (1990). The rocky road from actions to intentions. Doctoral dissertation, Stanford University.
Heath, C. & Heath, D. (2007). Made to Stick. Random House (두드리기 실험 소개)
청소 회사, 철물점, 소프트웨어 팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Newton(1990) 실험 수치 확인 필요: 두드린 곡 120곡 중 듣는 사람이 맞힌 곡은 3곡(2.5%, 약 40분의 1), 두드린 사람의 예상은 약 50%. 2차 자료(Made to Stick)에 널리 인용된 수치이므로 원 논문으로 다시 확인하세요.
Dana, Marcus, 소프트웨어 팀 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 해당 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: Two texts, one Monday: why one team did the right job
body: Dana runs a home cleaning company. Marcus runs a hardware store. On the same Monday, each needs their team to fix a problem, and each sends a short text.
One team does exactly the right thing by mid-afternoon. The other works hard all day and gets it wrong again. Nobody was lazy.

image.label: Two phones showing two different text messages
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나란히 놓인 휴대폰 두 대. 왼쪽 화면에는 흐릿한 긴 말풍선, 오른쪽 화면에는 번호가 붙은 짧고 선명한 말풍선. 배경에 왼쪽은 청소 도구, 오른쪽은 철물점 선반. 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A client is upset. What do you text your crew?
body: You run a home cleaning company. A client called: last visit, the crew skipped her upstairs guest bathroom and used the wrong spray on her marble countertop.
The same crew goes back tomorrow. Which text do you send the crew lead?

options.text: "The Parkers were really unhappy last time. Please be extra careful tomorrow and make it perfect."
options.feedback: It shows you care and keeps things friendly. But it says how to feel, not what to do, so the crew may work harder on the wrong things.

options.text: "At the Parkers tomorrow: clean the upstairs guest bathroom, and use only the pH-neutral spray on the kitchen marble. Text me a photo of both."
options.feedback: Two exact actions and a way to confirm them. It takes you a minute longer to write and saves the crew from guessing.

options.text: A full account of the client's call, every complaint in order, ending with "so keep all that in mind."
options.feedback: All the facts are there, which beats a vague text. But the crew lead has to dig out the actions, and may pick the wrong ones.

cards.title: Same effort, different results.
body: Dana sent something like option A. Her crew spent an extra hour scrubbing the kitchen floor. The guest bathroom was skipped again.
Marcus texted: "Snow Thursday. By 6pm Wednesday, move shovels and ice melt to the endcap by the front door. Send me a photo." It was done by 4pm.
Dana's crew wasn't careless. They did their best with a message that only made sense inside Dana's head.

image.label: Cleaner scrubbing a floor while a bathroom door stays shut; store worker stacking shovels by the door
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽: 청소부가 땀 흘리며 부엌 바닥을 닦고, 뒤쪽 욕실 문은 닫혀 있음. 오른쪽: 철물점 직원이 입구 옆 진열대에 눈삽과 제설제를 쌓고 사진을 찍음. 상표나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Clear communication
body: A message is **clear** when the person receiving it can act on it correctly without coming back to ask you anything.
That test is about the reader, not the writer. Dana knew which bathroom was skipped and which spray was wrong. To her, "be extra careful" pointed straight at both. To her crew, it pointed everywhere.
Psychologists call this the **curse of knowledge**: once you know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it.

cards.title: What Marcus's text did in 20 words.
body: Each part answers a question the team would otherwise have to ask.

breakdown.label: Point first
breakdown.detail: Move the winter stock, before any background

breakdown.label: Exact action
breakdown.detail: Shovels and ice melt, to the front endcap

breakdown.label: What done looks like
breakdown.detail: A photo of the finished display

cards.title: Tap a song. Hear it. They don't.
body: In a 1990 Stanford study, Elizabeth Newton asked people to tap out the rhythm of well-known songs, like "Happy Birthday", on a table. Listeners tried to name each song.
Tappers expected listeners to get about half right. Listeners got **about 1 in 40**.
The tappers heard the melody in their heads as they tapped. The listeners heard only knocking. Every vague instruction works the same way.

image.label: A person tapping a table with music notes above their head; the listener hears only dots
image.brief: 두 사람이 테이블에 마주 앉음. 두드리는 사람 머리 위에는 음표가 가득한 말풍선, 듣는 사람 머리 위에는 '톡 톡 톡' 점만 있는 말풍선. 따뜻한 색감, 단순한 일러스트.

cards.title: Clear is not the same as short.
body: Cut too much and you lose the why. If a delivery blocks Marcus's endcap, a team that knows "snow is coming" finds another spot by the door. A team with only an order waits for him.
And no message is clear until someone acts on it. For anything that matters, check what people plan to do, not just whether they got the text.
Clarity is for instructions and decisions. Emotional conversations need more than a tidy list.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: You lead a five-person team. This week, three customers were charged twice after tapping "Pay" twice. You release on Friday.
Which message do you post in the team chat?

options.text: "Payments feel a bit fragile lately. Can we tighten things up before Friday?"
options.feedback: Low-pressure and polite, but everyone will picture a different problem. You may get five small fixes and not the one you need.

options.text: "Before Friday: stop double charges when users tap Pay twice. Priya owns it. Done means a test that taps twice and charges once. Why: three customers hit this."
options.feedback: Action, owner, deadline, finish line and reason. The rest of the team also knows they can keep working on their own tasks.

options.text: "Double-charge bug is top priority. Everyone drop what you're doing and look at payments."
options.feedback: The priority is clear. But with no owner, five people may collide on one fix while the rest of Friday's release stalls.

cards.title: A message is clear when they can act without asking you.
body: Put the point first. Name the action, the owner and the deadline. Add one line of why, and say what done looks like.
**Try it today:** before you send your next instruction, reread it as the person getting it. What question would they need to ask? Answer it in the message.
